description:
We are TerraMappers, a student team exploring how our home planet can help humanity prepare for life beyond Earth. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we’re using Earth, Moon, and Mars data to identify environments on Earth that could help researchers test technologies and plan future missions. Combining coding, research, and creative problem-solving, we aim to turn complex planetary data into an accessible tool for discovery.

Exploring Earth. Preparing for new worlds.
summary:
Celestra is a web platform that identifies Earth locations resembling proposed Moon and Mars base sites, helping users choose where to test mission hardware and understand which conditions those tests can reproduce.
Using NASA and ESA satellite data, it compares terrain, surface texture, ground cover and available temperature measurements. Only properties measured at both sites contribute to each score. Rather than selecting one universally “best” analogue, Celestra recommends locations for specific hardware tests and explains the limits of each match.
Our deep ensemble of neural networks screened 48,492 patches of Earth’s bare land while estimating prediction uncertainty. Re-measuring promising candidates with higher-resolution elevation data added 163 new sites to our rankings; 44 of them outscore every site on our curated reference list for at least one destination. 
A paired 3D simulator lets users explore rover driving, landing and drilling on Earth and corresponding planetary terrain. Together, these tools help researchers, engineers and students select more relevant test environments, investigate potential hardware weaknesses and prepare for lunar and Martian exploration.
details:
1. What we developed

Celestra helps engineers find Earth environments suitable for testing hardware intended for the Moon or Mars. Users can pick one of 28 suggested destinations on the Moon and Mars, or click anywhere on either globe.

The platform ranks 166 Earth locations for lunar comparisons and 136 for Martian comparisons, combining established analogue sites with AI-discovered candidates. It also recommends sites for seven hardware test categories, recognizing that a suitable rover test site may not be suitable for a lander.

2. How we compare locations

We analyse a 2 × 2 km area around each site using satellite measurements of terrain slope, roughness, surface texture and, where available, daytime and nighttime temperatures.

Measurements are converted to a common scale and combined into a similarity score from 0 to 100, with a visible breakdown. Only properties available for both sites contribute; missing measurements are excluded rather than estimated. Comparisons currently use ten properties for the Moon and seven for Mars. Vegetation and water reduce a site’s suitability.

As a basic benchmark test, we tested eight unsuitable environments, including rainforests, swamps and farmland, on the 28 destinations. These eight environments consistently ranked the lowest due to lack of vegetation and water on Moon and Mars, thus proving the model's reliability.

3. How we discover new sites

Our processing combines NASA’s LOLA, Diviner, HiRISE and MODIS data with Copernicus elevation data and Sentinel-2 imagery. A separate model estimates sunlight exposure near the lunar poles.

To search beyond established sites, we trained seven neural networks on different samples of approximately 2,400 detailed locations. They use coarser global data to predict similarity scores. Their predictions are averaged, while disagreement helps estimate uncertainty. Conformal prediction adds uncertainty intervals with a target coverage of 90%.

The ensemble screened 48,492 bare-land patches. We then measured the top 280 candidates using higher-resolution data, identifying 62 that scored above the established reference sites in their respective comparisons. Final rankings use measured scores, rather than AI predictions.

4. Paired mission simulation

Users can land a spacecraft, drive a rover, collect rocks and drill cores on Earth and corresponding lunar or Martian terrain generated from elevation data.

The simulator models differences in gravity and atmosphere to explore effects such as slipping, sliding and motor cooling. It illustrates which aspects of Earth testing may transfer to another celestial body.

5. Current limitations

  • Planetary mineral composition and Martian temperatures are currently excluded.
  • Terrain analysis cannot resolve individual boulders.
  • Limited HiRISE coverage restricts live Mars comparisons.
  • The nominal 90% prediction intervals achieved 90% coverage on held-out tests and 78% during candidate verification, indicating a need for further evaluation.
  • Our team selected the control sites. Independent field validation remains a priority.

6. Technologies Used

Data:

  1. NASA Planetary Data System (LRO LOLA, LRO Diviner, MRO HiRISE)
  2. NASA Worldview (MODIS)
  3. ESA Copernicus DEM, Sentinel-2

Software:

  1. Python (FastAPI, NumPy, pandas, rasterio/GDAL)
  2. PyTorch
  3. TypeScript (Next.js, React, Three.js)

Deployment:

Docker, Render. Can be run in any modern browser.

7. Future Goals

Celestra supports field planning through explainable recommendations and printable campaign briefs. It also gives students an accessible way to investigate mission preparation. We aim to add Martian temperature and planetary mineral datasets, and incorporate official Artemis region boundaries.
